This seems like a great idea implemented about as terribly as humanly possible. What they mention about the commercial possibilities leading to greater quality mods for players is certainly true. I'm an independent developer and have actually been pretty interested in contributing to modding, particularly related to VR. Instead I have to focus the vast majority of my attention on commercial projects. Player gratitude doesn't pay the bills. I'm sure plenty of other developers are in a similar situation. Commercialized mods could even allow more traditionally employed developers, who work on mods in their spare time, to begin to work on their mods fulltime if they were well received. Awesome for players and modders.

But to start with the lack of any sort of basic barrier to entry is just insane. Thousands of people selling non-content or blatantly stealing intellectual property from others is incredibly predictable when you completely open it up. Require a "commercial license" that costs $100, or the regionally adjusted equivalent, to post commercial workshop content. The license is permanent and applies to all games. It is only revoked in cases of breaking the terms of the commercial workshop which most obviously would include listing content that you don't clearly own the rights to. And just like that, 99% of the opportunist-come-scammers are gone.

There's also the issue of the people who actually create everything only get a 25% "share." That is simply exploitative and effectively negates everything I said about this possibly bringing in more professional style development to mods. Aside from the fact that Bethesda is taking 45% of a windfall for doing literally nothing that they weren't already, it simply removes the motivation for anything other than quick little money grabs. You don't want to spend thousands of hours developing interesting content without any sort of professional support (assets, product support, testing/QA, etc) whatsoever only to see 3 out of 4 of your sales go, in their entirety, to Bethesda/Steam. The reason Steam became popular with developers in the first place was their decision to eschew traditional screw-the-people-who-actually-make-the-product deals, like this one. This is regressive and while it may appeal to modders who are happy just to be able to monetize their product which they were already making for free, it makes claiming that this monetization will actively attract outside professional developers a completely disingenuous argument.

The thing is, modding is a hobby, always has been. It's not a creation of your own, it's playing with Lego. Monetizing it allows software companies that are already incredibly lazy, like Bethesda, to be even more lazy. It also encourages potentially talented developers to be incredibly lazy and never take the step of learning how to create something from scratch. Paid for building with Lego, how sweet.

This is a dark chapter for the gaming industry in my opinion. Not only do they squeeze every last drop from the customer with over priced unfinished games that come with over priced DLC, now they want those same people to actually do their job for them and create more content and make money out of that too. Fuck that.

Sadly it just keeps getting worse and no matter how much people yell about it on the internet nothing will change. Sometimes I feel like the only thing to do is kiss the old ways goodbye, accept that things are going to be working differently from now on, and become an even bigger pirate then before.

Many modders have modded for reasons well beyond just a fun hobby. The example that comes to mind immediately is Velicky. He was a 19 year old who spent thousands of hours developing a DLC quality mod for Skyrim - Falskaar. His goal was overtly to try to get a job in the games industry. And it succeeded. Bungie snapped him up fast. The sad thing is he just sold himself seriously short and that's pretty typical when people don't understand the value of what they're doing and creating. He's now entered a career that he will likely hate. The games industry isn't the dream job most think it is, even if you love games. In a few years he'll likely come out bitter and jaded with very little financially to show for it when he clearly has the skills and drive to do big things on his own.

Other modders actually had a bit more business sense and realized their value. Defense of the Ancients, which sparked the whole multi billion dollar MOBA craze, was a mod. There a number of the developers realized the potential commercialization and segued naturally into such. But obtaining VC capitalization, starting a new business, marketing - these things aren't things for everybody. Half Life Counter-Strike is a tale with a less happy ending. It also started as a mod and became one of the most played and well regarded shooter franchises of all time. There the devs did not manage to segue their mod into commercial success. Instead they sold their rights away for a pittance and went to go work for other people.

The point here being that there's no real reason for mods to be a stepping stone as opposed to an ends in and of themselves. It's been decades since people "created things from scratch." For instance even if you build your own engine, you're not actually. Each time the developer makes a single call to OpenGL or Direct3D it is doing an enormous amount of work behind the scenes built for them by other people, that devs used to have to manually do. The same is true of sound, input and every single other user experience API.

I completely agree with you on the decline of the traditional gaming industry and that's actually one of the reasons I support this idea. It allows smaller scale development teams to utilize extensive, if unfulfilled, frameworks (which is exactly how I'd describe Skyrim) to actually create amazing content and experiences for users. And these devs can actually do this while supporting themselves at the same time instead of having to run a day job and work themselves senseless just to be able to build what they want to.

Very very off topic, but this also why I am a huge supporter of unconditional basic income which you can find out more about at /r/BasicIncome. I'm not some mad raving greedy capitalist, just pragmatic. The software world would explode in creativity if we weren't all being hamstrung to the requirement of having to make a buck on everything we create.

I hear what you're saying about nothing really being created from scratch anymore but come on, modding (especially with Skyrim) is MUCH simpler then anything else and I think that you are giving those modders far too much credit and value. How Photography Was Optimized for White Skin Color
It's an interesting article, but it seems they want to equate limited dynamic range with some sort of intrinsic racism and I'm not sure I agree with that.

They are making connections that, in my opinion, are quite a stretch. The "Shirley" standard photograph can be explained by making sure that you have the proper separation of the darkest blacks and brightest whites without blowing highlights or losing detail in the shadows, it wouldn't matter the color of the skin, that just happens to be their white point for that photograph. Also, the chemistry for film, and sensors in digital cameras, are balanced so that they can represent as true color as the eye sees as possible. Obviously there are exceptions to this rule for various things such as x-processing or something where you are trying to throw the color pallet off from it's normal choices, but in general are going to capture what it sees with pretty accurate results.

edit: Source: Film photographer who develops and prints in a home darkroom.
